newsitem.title: USA: Ease controls on US food sales to N.Korea-Senators.
newsitem.headline: Ease controls on US food sales to N.Korea-Senators.

text.p: Four U.S. senators, fresh from a trip to North Korea, said Friday the United States should ease its restrictions on food sales to North Korea as a way to relieve the threat of widespread starvation.
During a news conference, the delegation described an alarming absence of livestock on farms near Pyongyang and a capital city so short of energy that streetlights were dark.
North Korean officials at first demanded 2.5 million tonnes of food aid as a precondition to four-party peace talks but backed off to requesting 500,000 tonnes, they said.
Sen. Ted Stevens, R-Alaska, who was delegation leader, said the group stressed that the way to better U.S.-North Korea relations was through the four-nation talks for peace on the Korean peninsula.

"We ought to encourage commercial (sales) of food into their area," Stevens said. Mississippi Republican Thad Cochran, Hawaii Democrat Daniel Inouye and Kansas Republican Pat Roberts nodded their agreement.
"Sell them anything they can't shoot back at us or over the DMZ (demilitarized zone)," Roberts said, paraphrasing a sentiment popular in the Farm Belt during the Cold War.

Humanitarian food aid should be channeled through the United Nations, Stevens said, and there were no requests for direct U.S. food aid at present. The U.S. "Food for Peace" program could handle small amounts but Stevens said a large request would require either a special appropriation or a change in U.S. foreign aid commitments.

The senators said they wanted to avert starvation, which might destablize the North Korean government or inspire a suicidal attack on South Korea. But they said North Korea's weapons programs were an obstacle.

Stevens refused to suggest how large a contribution the United States should make to a U.N. request for additional food. So far, the U.S. has contributed $18.4 million since late 1995, including $10 million in food en route to North Korea.

Roberts said a zinc-for-wheat barter arranged by U.S. grain giant Cargill Inc was a first step to developing commercial food trade. Cargill was authorized by the Treasury Department to sell up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice.
North Korea has valuable minerals, like diamonds and magnesium, that could be bartered, Stevens said.
Sen. Pete Domenici, R-N.M., who also made the trip, said North Korea was "desperately short of energy. Their buildings are only half-lit. There are no street lights...no automobiles on the roads."

Cochran said there was a somber mood on Pyongyang's streets and, during a visit to a communal farm near the capital, "there was no activity....There was no livestock, ducks, pigs or chickens in sight."
"We didn't see any farm animals, not even a water buffalo. Our conclusion was they ate all of them," Stevens said.
According to estimates, North Korea will fall more than two million tonnes short of its food needs this year.
Roberts said he met earlier in the day with Cargill officials. They were waiting to see if the zinc barter bore fruit before seeking additional deals, he said.
"They should know in 30 days," Roberts said.
